b: Cold weather impacts marine Lithium Iron Phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries in two main ways. For anglers, the difference lies in whether you’re using the batteries on the water or plugging them into a charger. Discharging (aka actively using) your batteries in freezing conditions causes a temporary dip in performance and runtime, whereas charging them while the internal cells are below freezing can cause irreversible damage.
Understanding the boundary between these two behaviors is the key to protecting your lithium batteries through the winter months.

“I’ve been running LiTime batteries in my tournament boat for the past two years, including through some challenging and unexpected winter weather,” said Jay “Striker” Barnett, a pro bass angler on the Major League Fishing Pro Circuit. “At our season opener in Florida, temperatures dropped into the low 20s. It was so cold that water pipes froze and burst overnight, something we certainly weren’t expecting in Florida. Later that season, we encountered snow at our third tournament stop in Alabama. Through both experiences, my LiTime batteries performed without an issue.”
LiTime has a built-in Battery Management System equipped with low-temperature charging protection that automatically blocks incoming current whenever cell temperatures drop below freezing.

When you are out fishing, you can safely run your trolling motor and electronics in temperatures all the way down to roughly -4°F (-20°C). Cold temperatures slow down the chemical reactions inside the battery and increase internal resistance, which translates on the water to a temporary 10 to 20 percent drop in usable capacity, according to Battery University and manufacturer discharge testing. The noticeable voltage sag really stands out when running a trolling motor on high or holding Spot-Lock in heavy current. Drawing power actually generates a small amount of internal heat that helps stabilize the cells while you fish, and once the battery warms back up, its full capacity returns with no lasting harm.

Charging is where cold weather becomes genuinely dangerous for lithium chemistry. You should never force a charge into a standard lithium battery when its internal cell temperature is below 32°F (0°C). Forcing electrical current into freezing cells prevents lithium ions from absorbing properly, causing metallic lithium to plate onto the anode instead, according to the Journal of Power Sources. This plating permanently destroys battery capacity and can eventually create internal short circuits.

“One of the biggest challenges with lithium batteries in cold weather is making sure the cells are at a safe temperature for charging,” said Striker. “As a professional angler, that matters because our tournament season starts during the winter months, and we often find ourselves fishing in freezing conditions and charging our batteries overnight before another long tournament day.”

To prevent this, quality marine lithium batteries rely on a built-in Battery Management System (BMS) equipped with low-temperature charging protection that automatically blocks incoming current whenever cell temperatures drop below freezing.

LiTime takes this a step further by integrating its built-in self-heating technology—known as LiHeat dual-mode self-heating system — across several deep-cycle LiFePO4 batteries, including 12V 100Ah Group 24, 12V 165Ah Dual Purpose, 12V 30Ah Self Heating Ice Fishing, and 16V 100Ah Self Heating options. Rather than simply preventing charging in freezing conditions, LiHeat actively warms the cells to a safe temperature range, enabling safe charging and dependable performance in cold weather.

When internal temperature sensors detect that the cells are between -4°F and 41°F (-20°C to 5°C), the battery’s upgraded Battery Management System (BMS) automatically blocks charging current from entering the cells and diverts that energy to dual internal heating pads instead. Depending on how cold the battery is, these pads warm the internal core to 50°F (10°C) in roughly 60 to 150 minutes, at which point the heating system shuts off and normal charging begins seamlessly.
In addition to standard charger-driven heating, LiTime’s smart self-heating batteries include a dual-mode system controlled through the LiTime mobile app.

Anglers can choose Regular Mode to warm the battery strictly via an external charger, or select Energy-Efficient Mode, which allows the battery to assist low-amperage chargers—or even preheat itself using its own stored power when above a 20% state of charge—to reduce warm-up times on freezing mornings. Flat out, neither mode allows charging while the cells remain below their permitted temperature range.

“All my LiTime batteries feature self-heating technology, including my two 165Ah smart dual-purpose marine batteries, which are connected in parallel to power my electronics and onboard electrical systems, and my two 36V 50Ah smart batteries that power my trolling motor,” explained Striker.

When a compatible external charger is connected to a cold battery, the system draws power from the charger to warm the cells before normal charging begins. This allows the battery to preheat without consuming its stored energy. Specific activation conditions depend on the battery model and charger.

In Energy-Efficient Mode, LiHeat allows users to initiate preheating remotely through the LiTime app, using energy stored in the battery. When the ambient temperature is above -20°C and the battery’s state of charge (SOC) is above 20%, users can activate self-heating in advance to warm the cells to a safe charging temperature. This allows charging to begin once a compatible charger is connected, reducing the waiting time typically required for the battery to warm up after connection.

Beyond thermal management, LiTime builds these packs with EV-grade prismatic cells rated for 4,000 to 6,000 cycles and a 10-year lifespan, pairing them with an IP65 waterproof housing and a BMS offering over 20 protections—including salt-spray resistance and moisture-proofing—to withstand harsh marine and winter fishing environments and temperatures.

Watch out for budget lithium batteries that omit the temperature sensor, meaning plugging in an onboard charger—or running an engine alternator’s charge-on-the-run system—on a freezing morning can ruin the pack. Even if daytime air warms up to 40°F, a heavy battery sitting in an insulated boat compartment overnight can retain a core temperature well below freezing, so ambient air temperature alone is not a reliable indicator that it is safe to charge.

If you are winterizing your rig for off-season storage rather than fishing through the cold, lithium batteries require a much simpler routine than traditional lead-acid models. Instead of storing them at 100% capacity hooked up to a continuous trickle charger, charge your lithium batteries to between 50% and 80% and leave them unhooked in a dry location anywhere between -4°F and 95°F. Because lithium batteries naturally self-discharge at a rate of only 1% to 3% per month, they will hold their charge until spring without any maintenance charging.

Even though the cells themselves barely lose charge over the winter, parasitic draws from boat accessories can still drain a battery completely over a few months and trip its low-voltage sleep mode. Before walking away from your boat for the winter, flip your main master breaker or physically disconnect the negative terminal from each battery. Trolling motors left in standby mode, bilge float switches, and even a battery’s own internal Bluetooth monitoring chip will steadily sip power if left connected.

For anglers who continue to fish through freezing weather or head out onto the ice, managing cold batteries comes down to a few practical adjustments. Small portable batteries used for ice fishing shuttles and forward-facing sonar can simply be brought inside the house to warm up for a couple of hours before plugging them into a wall charger. If you keep large trolling motor batteries mounted inside an unheated boat or garage all winter, consider upgrading to self-heating lithium batteries—which automatically divert incoming charger power to internal heating pads until the cells reach about 41°F.
